title: Trump's redistricting gave Republicans a head start, now it goes to the voters
description: Voters across much of the South are casting ballots ahead of next month's midterm elections in congressional districts that were redrawn follow
body:
Voters across much of the South are casting ballots ahead of next month's midterm elections in congressional districts that were redrawn following calls from President Trump. He said it would help the GOP hold the House, where they currently outnumber Democrats 218 to 214.   In state legislatures over the last year, Republicans tilted about eight more seats their way than Democrats did in response. (That's an estimate, shown on the bar graph below.)   
   But it's the voters who will decide whether it works.    Here's the catch: Republicans redrew districts partly on how people voted in the presidential election in 2024. Now the political mood has changed and many who voted for President Trump two years ago could be voting for Democrats, or not voting, in the midterms. The Republicans could lose many of the districts they targeted.   Usually, states redistrict early in each decade after the census. But Trump called on legislatures to do it now. It set off a chain reaction of political crises across the country that threw legislatures into the national spotlight.   
   Texas Republicans issued arrest warrants for Democratic legislators who'd left the state. The Louisiana governor suspended a primary after thousands of votes were already cast so the lines could be redrawn. In Missouri, the state supreme court found the Republican secretary of state in contempt for sticking with a GOP map that was not legally in effect.   
   In California and Virginia, Democrats won approval in statewide votes for redistricting in response to the Republicans in other states – only to have the courts toss out Virginia's plan. And when the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act this spring, it fueled rushed legislative sessions to draw maps that often ended up weakening the voting power of minority communities.   In a few places, Republicans rejected Trump's call to redistrict, including dramatic votes in the Indiana and South Carolina legislatures. But overall, Trump prompted a cycle of mid-decade redistricting unlike any since the 1960s, when courts set the current rules.   Here's where states redistricted - or didn't.    Loading...

title: Farm country has beef with Trump as midterms approach
description: Cattle feed at a ranch in Dublin, Texas,
body:
Cattle feed at a ranch in Dublin, Texas, on September 11, 2026.
                
                    RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP for Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP for Getty Images
    

   
   Driving around his farm in a four-wheeler, Scott Birker warned that his cattle were in a bad mood.   "They're a little grumpy with me right now," he said.   When asked why, he said matter-of-factly: "We just got done weaning."    Birker should know his herd well, given that he's been raising beef cattle outside the Eastern Iowa town of Garrison since 2001. His operation has about 150 "mama cows" and sells feeder calves, as well as some cattle for meat. And Birker is also the northeast regional vice president for the Iowa Cattlemen's Association.   All of which is to say that since August, when Trump announced that his administration would raise the quota on beef imported under lower tariffs – temporarily suspending tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported beef – Birker knows it when he says: that hurt people.   
   "That surprise, with a very volatile market already, with a tight supply, hurts us really, really fast and really, really hard," Birker said.   It's not that raising beef cattle was easy before that new import policy. Margins are always tight, says Zach Raff, incoming livestock economist at Iowa State University. But there have also been other challenges – for example, drought in much of the western U.S. made hay much more expensive and shrank the nation's beef herd.   "The beef herd size is at an all time low – a 75-year-low," said Raff. "So you couple that with very strong demand. And that's going to make prices what you see at the store right now."   Ground beef currently costs around $6.80 a pound – a fact of which the Trump administration is keenly aware. But the administration's attempts to bring those prices down have backfired politically and possibly economically..   Multiple Trump administration policies have made life tougher for beef producers. Last year, amid the trade war between the two countries, China cut its US beef purchases. In February, Trump signed an executive order to subject some Argentinian beef to fewer tariffs.   And in August, he signed the executive order to suspend tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of beef imports – specifically, lean beef trimmings, with the goal of lowering the price of ground beef. The order added that the imported beef was to be sold at 25% below market prices.   
   That helped push U.S. cattle prices lower, but the far bigger challenge, according to Raff, was the amount of uncertainty it introduced.   "If I'm a producer, I think, well, look what's happening – perhaps next year they're going to import even more. The year after, there's going to be a different policy," said Raff. "And I'm going to say, 'Well, these prices for my cattle right now are at record highs and projected to be high. So I'm just going to send my heifers to be processed.' I'm not going to decide to replace the beef herd when I know that there's a lot of uncertainty."   This means the beef imports can have an added downside, disincentivizing producers from keeping breeding stock around that could grow the beef herd, which would lower beef prices in the long run.   Big picture    From an economics 101 perspective, the Trump decision to import more beef does make sense as a way of bringing down consumer prices. But the 300,000 metric tons that could be exempted from tariffs is equivalent to around 2% of total US beef consumption.   That made for a lose-lose situation: the policy was enough to rattle beef producers, but not enough to help consumers. Indeed, the average ground beef price per pound in September was only about 13 cents lower than it was in August.   All of this looms over the 2026 midterm elections, especially in farm states such as Iowa. Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running for the state's open Senate seat, made news when she publicly broke with the Trump administration on its decision to lower tariffs on beef imports.   "We need to focus on affordability, but I think this isn't the way to do that," she said on Fox News. "I think we need to focus on helping our cattlemen grow their herd."   
   Her opponent, Democratic state legislator Josh Turek, has in turn been stressing that Hinson has supported some Trump policies that have hurt farmers writ large.   "She's been in favor of all this five times in favor of the tariffs," he said in an interview with NPR. "Farmers rely on markets, on free trade, more than any other group."   In the governor's race, similarly, Democratic state auditor Rob Sand has sharply criticized Trump's trade policies, while Republican businessman Zach Lahn has avoided that kind of criticism.   Iowa Republican strategist David Oman says that in either race, the beef policy could be a deciding factor.   "Both of them will be two- or three-, four-point races in my view," he said. "So any one element like this topic that cuts against you hurts."   Indeed, the administration has been playing defense on the beef policy from the beginning. Speaking in Iowa just days after the beef executive order, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins acknowledged that the August order lifting the beef tariff rate quotas, or TRQs, might not be popular.   "I believe everyone will look back on this time and say, okay, didn't love the three month lift of the TRQ, but we're so grateful to a president that is willing to listen, willing to make big, bold decisions, and willing to put it all out there for our American producers," she said at the Iowa Farm Progress Show.   How it plays   Seth Watkins, who has his own cattle herd in southwestern Iowa, outside the town of Clarinda, says that these trade decisions make him upset not only with Trump, but with all of Washington.   "As much as what the president does frustrates me, I think I'm more frustrated with Congress, who should be exercising the checks and balances we learned about in high school civics," he said.   
   He's a Democrat and going to vote blue in this election, though he says he doesn't blame other farmers who have supported Trump.   "They honestly were told that tariffs were going to make markets better," he said. "They were told that we were going to enter this new golden era. I just filled up my pickup with $6.30 diesel fuel."   This is not just about Iowa. Several states with some of the tightest races this year – Texas, Nebraska, Montana, and Kansas – are also major beef-producing states, meaning lots of people weighing these particular trade policies as they vote.   Back on his farm, Birker knows how he'll vote, too: "I'll vote Republican."   Birker stresses that this is purely a personal decision, and that the Iowa Cattlemen are a non partisan group. But for his part, he generally votes Republican, and getting to talk personally to Hinson also reinforced his choice.   As for Trump, Birker approves of how he's doing as president.   "I do, I do," he said. "I just think it's a long putt. He's a businessman, and I think we've got to stick it out with him."   Trump will have the opportunity to convince more Iowans when he travels to Sioux City this week as part of his pre-midterm push.

title: Federal judge restricts DHS field operations looking for noncitizen voters
description: People vote at a polling location at Los
body:
People vote at a polling location at Los Angeles' Metro Headquarters Building during California's state primary on June 2, 2026.
                
                    Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   A federal judge in California is putting limits on pre-election field operations conducted by the Department of Homeland Security that the agency says is aimed at trying to find noncitizens who have illegally voted in nine states.   In recent weeks, armed Homeland Security Investigations officers have carried out field operations and visited homes to interview people suspected of illegally voting as noncitizens. The targets can include people who became citizens but voted before they naturalized.   In a 19-page order late Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, an appointee of President Joe Biden, wrote that the federal government was using "flawed" data in the initiative and that its efforts likely violated the Voting Rights Act, which bars voter intimidation.   
   Martínez-Olguín referenced a disclosure last month from a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services whistleblower that alleged rushed efforts to match data to create a target list of potential noncitizens on voter rolls, and that the list includes U.S. citizens. She also pointed to HSI's social media posts, including one that showed agents handcuffing a California man accused of unlawfully registering to vote.   
   The judge wrote that the government's use of unreliable and incomplete data along with highly publicized arrests "lead to an objectively reasonable fear of law enforcement entanglements that intimidates citizens from urging or aiding others in exercising their right to vote."   HSI field operations were planned in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin, according to documents produced in the case and CNN reporting.   Martínez-Olguín barred DHS officers in those states from conducting field operations targeting people they "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens," or that are based "wholly" on USCIS matching data without further investigation.   In a declaration, USCIS official Nicolas Bartell had told the judge his team manually reviews records before referring them to HSI, but acknowledged the "low possibility" citizens could be "erroneously identified as potential aliens" in federal records. He wrote the risks were mitigated by safeguards his office takes "and any remaining risks were outweighed by the need to support the agency's law-enforcement and election-integrity mission."   
   It's unclear how much of an effect the judge's order will have on the federal government's highly publicized campaign to find noncitizen voters.   States reviews and audits have consistently found voting by noncitizens to be extremely rare.   "DHS is laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens. ONLY Americans should elect American leaders," the agency wrote in a statement. "We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens."   The order is set to take effect on Friday and would be in effect through election night, though the federal government could appeal.   The judge's ruling came in a lawsuit filed last month by a coalition that includes San Francisco and Santa Clara counties, the city of San Francisco, nursing unions and Voto Latino Foundation. Protect Democracy and the National Immigration Law Center are litigating the case against the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice.   "Today, the courts affirmed a vital principle of our democracy: Voting is a fundamental right that citizens — whether born here or naturalized — should be able to exercise without armed government agents harassing them," Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer with Protect Democracy, said in a statement.   "It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people's homes weeks before an election," he added.   A court filing by the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United described naturalized citizen members who no longer wanted to attend political rallies, sign up to be election poll workers, or vote in person because of the federal operations.   The order comes as the Department of Justice is suing California and demanding the state segregate 20,000 ballots from people federal officials say they believe are "likely" noncitizens.   
   A preliminary review of a sample of that list by Los Angeles County election officials found many of the registrations were canceled, inactive or had no voting history, and some pertained to people who indicated they were born in the U.S.   The DOJ announced charges against 28 green card holders across the state on Monday who are accused of illegally voting or registering to vote.

title: Trump's attacks on the press have become a war
description: The New York Times reported that the Trump Administration is considering physically moving the White House press corps out of the White House.
body:
The New York Times reported that the Trump Administration is considering physically moving the White House press corps out of the White House.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  When he ran for president first back in 2016, Donald Trump would often get the audience at his rallies to boo all of the reporters in unison. As President Trump, he has continued to berate the journalists who cover him. But this year, his actions toward the press corps have been more than verbal attacks. Just this week, in fact, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration is considering physically moving the White House press corps out of the White House. The White House counsel also sent a letter to Politico this week telling them to retract stories or face consequences.We're going to talk about all this with Ruth Marcus, a longtime Washington Post columnist, now a contributor for The New Yorker. Thanks for coming on.RUTH MARCUS: Thanks for for having me.DETROW: Let's start with this New York Times reporting. As we know, as we've talked about on this show, the White House is already trying to limit some White House access for major outlets like The Associated Press, like CNN with those legal cases ongoing. But Trump has reportedly told his staff he wants to get rid of the White House briefing room. He wants to turn it back into the pool that it was during the Roosevelt administration. What, to you, would that mean? How serious would that be?MARCUS: Well, it would be serious, but it would all - and I think you're totally right. In the second Trump administration, he has operationalized the animus towards the press. But I do want to say, though, that many presidents, Republican and Democrat, have been frustrated with the media coverage that they've gotten. And they have also toyed with/fantasized about the notion of moving those pesky reporters out of the White House.DETROW: Yeah, yeah.MARCUS: OK? This would be petty. It would be vindictive. It would be bad for the media, but it wouldn't actually be that helpful for the president. Yes, it would get reporters out of your hair. But look at the experience that Pete Hegseth, the secretary of - I say - defense has had since he kicked reporters out of the Pentagon. It has not stopped Pentagon reporting. Reporters are going to report. Even if you kick them physically out of the space...DETROW: Yeah.MARCUS: ...They are not going to stop doing their jobs, full stop.DETROW: So obviously, that would be a symbolic move. It would have some repercussions. Like you said, reporting would continue anyway. That all being said, what, to you, are the one or two most frightening, most concerning actual steps taken? Because, like I said, I feel like we've gotten numb to President Trump criticizing the press, but it's gone far beyond that lately.MARCUS: Well, you know, if you only surround yourself or expose yourself to questions from reporters who are, say, fawning over your presidency or in line with your ideology, you are not going to get tough questions from the media, and that is not just a problem for us as reporters. It's a problem for the public that relies on us to ask tough questions. That's No. 1. No. 2, I would say, is the threat of using government power to punish especially broadcasters who've...DETROW: Yeah, this is through FCC direct threats or investigations or lawsuits over coverage and seeing networks settle or then clearly water down their coverage in response.MARCUS: Exactly. And I would combine that with these frivolous but still expensive and energy-sucking defamation suits.DETROW: We saw the Justice Department, in trying to investigate leaks over the new Air Force One gift that Trump got and the problems with it, we saw them show up at reporter for The New York Times homes. Though that's something the federal courts pushed back on. Given that track record, what did you make of what's been going on with Politico this week. Politico reported - what was interesting to me is it's just kind of, like, staff-level gossip. It's about the chief of staff and the president, so it's of note, but still it's not anything that you could claim is national security. And yet there's this fierce response and the promise of a threat from the White House counsel toward Politico. What did you make of that?MARCUS: I thought it was astonishing, in particular, that the White House counsel, whose job is fundamentally to represent the president but also to uphold the Constitution, was threatening Politico if it failed to retract its story. Politico made a mistake in the story. It corrected that mistake. But there is no basis or cause that I'm aware of to call on Politico to retract its story. And this is part of what should be the normal give-and-take and the normal tensions that are going to occur between any administration and any set of reporters covering them. But in this administration, it has been ratcheted up...DETROW: Yeah.MARCUS: ...In a way that I think doesn't serve the administration's interests in the end, but it certainly doesn't serve the public interest.DETROW: I'm curious what you make of the dynamic that Trump is certainly much louder, much more aggressive, much more likely to follow up his threats with actions than other previous presidents, and yet he seems to be the most media-attuned president we've probably ever had. How do you think about that symbiotic relationship that still exists even with all of these threats?MARCUS: The most media-attuned and also the most media-accessible. He thrives on that - the hostile interchanges that he has with reporters, but he also needs the attention. And when there were those couple dark days when the pool balked at covering him because he had excluded people from the pool, that's like cutting off Trump's oxygen. So in the end, he needs us as - you know, at least as much as we need him. We can do our jobs calling White House sources, reporting behind the scenes, but if we're not there, we're not serving as his foils and we're not serving as his amplifiers.DETROW: That is Ruth Marcus, contributor for The New Yorker. Thank you so much.MARCUS: Thank you for having me.

title: U.S., Israel may attack Iran post-elections. And, SpaceX and Tesla consider merging
description:
Democratic Surrogates Campaign, US & Israel Plan Iran Strikes, Tesla SpaceX Merger
    
            
                
                Tr
body:
Democratic Surrogates Campaign, US & Israel Plan Iran Strikes, Tesla SpaceX Merger
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-149315/nx-s1-mx-6012014-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   President Trump isn't the only one hitting key states in the last days before the midterm elections. Democrats are bringing out big names, too. Former President Barack Obama will be in Ohio and Michigan this weekend, and next week he heads to Georgia. Today, former Vice President Kamala Harris is set to visit Mississippi, which has a surprisingly competitive Senate race.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                People walk by a polling place at Denver's Central Library on June 30, 2026.
                
                    Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 Many Democrats are visiting toss-up and deep-red areas across the country, NPR's Stephen Fowler tells Up First. Alongside figures like Obama and Harris, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Sen. Cory Booker and former DNC chair Jaime Harrison are going to different states to help with campaigning. Fowler says these leaders resemble a shadow primary for potential 2028 presidential candidates. He also notes that the Democrats' campaign push is happening against a backdrop of a big surge in Black voter turnout during early voting.➡️ The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) announced yesterday that it will no longer issue endorsements, make direct PAC contributions or earmark funds for candidates. The influential lobbying group began its direct political involvement five years ago but has faced growing resistance and criticism over its positions on issues like the wars in Gaza and Iran.➡️ This week, the Department of Justice started notifying the counties it wants to monitor on Election Day, NPR has learned. The DOJ deploys monitors to ensure compliance with voting laws, but officials have raised concerns this year over the Trump administration's efforts to control elections.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.   
   The U.S. and Israel are preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran early next month, a person briefed on the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity so they could discuss the preparations, told NPR today. This potential strike would occur after the U.S. midterm elections and Israel's elections next week. The development comes after Israeli security forces in the occupied West Bank detained about 80 people yesterday, including U.S. Democratic congressional nominee for New York Brad Lander and more than a dozen American rabbis.   🎧 Israel initially intended to strike Iran in mid-October, but Trump objected, according to NPR's source. These preparations might aim to pressure Iran into a diplomatic deal, NPR's Ruth Sherlock says. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is campaigning to topple Iran's regime, and if election results remain uncertain by November, he may use the threat of military action to form a unity government.   Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a merger. Together, Elon Musk's two companies would potentially amplify his influence as one of the wealthiest individuals on Earth. The new company would become one of the largest globally, boasting a combined market cap of approximately $3.7 trillion.   🎧 Musk revived the idea of a merger this week during recent SpaceX and Tesla earnings calls, according to NPR's John Ruwitch. If it proceeds, analysts believe Musk could gain a controlling share in Tesla, where he currently wields less voting power compared to SpaceX, Ruwitch says. In November, Tesla shareholders approved a trillion-dollar pay package for Musk, contingent on meeting growth targets over the next decade. This merger could help him achieve those targets and secure the payout. Shareholders must approve the deal, but analysts believe this could be challenging on Tesla's side because shareholders might demand a higher share price.   
   Today's listen   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Cardi B performing at the NPR Tiny Desk.
                
                    NPR Tiny Desk
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        NPR Tiny Desk
    

   
   When news broke that Cardi B would be at the NPR Music office, so many people came to see the rapper perform an intimate set that staff had to turn some away, which is a rare occurrence. People flocked to see the unfiltered rap star, who arrived in leather pants and a power blazer, bringing a mix of humility and humor. She opened her performance with the haunting synths of "Hello" and closed with two pivotal hits from her catalog: the breakout single "Bodak Yellow" and the boogaloo-heavy "I Like It." Don't miss out — catch her entire electrifying Tiny Desk Concert here.   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Chip Thomas, a retired physician on the Navajo Reservation, is well known for his large photograhpic murals. Now, he's been recognized with a MacArthur "genius" grant.
                
                    John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation
    

   
   Chip Thomas has been creating public art in rural areas of the Navajo Nation for nearly two decades. Last month, he received a MacArthur Foundation "genius" award for the social impact of his work. His artwork features large black-and-white images depicting life on the reservation. Thomas moved to the Navajo Nation in 1987 as a family physician and grew close to the community, helping with everyday tasks and eventually started photographing them. His art reflects the beauty and resilience of the people who live on the land. Don't miss these stunning photos.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Gary Tyler speaks about his work at the Grand Rapids Art Museum in Michigan. Behind Tyler are his quilts Big Toe, (2024) and Enduring, (2025). They feature two individuals who are incarcerated. He hopes his work draws attention to their plight and humanity.
                
                    Sea Stachura for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Sea Stachura for NPR
    

   
   Gary Tyler, a quilt artist who spent decades on death row for a murder he did not commit, now has his first solo exhibit at the Grand Rapids Art Museum.Researchers are publishing some of the first data in humans suggesting that psilocybin may have potential benefits for patients with neurodegenerative diseases, such as Parkinson's.America has a new national park. Trump signed legislation this week upgrading the status of Arizona's Chiricahua National Monument. The park is part of the Chiricahua Mountains. (via AZPM)   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'
description: The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., a Phil
body:
The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., a Philadelphia suburb, closed early this year amid falling sales.
                
                    Frank Langfitt/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frank Langfitt/NPR
    

   
   BENSALEM, Pa. – When the Trump merchandise store here announced it was closing earlier this year, Wes Alker, a Trump superfan and retired auto mechanic, came by for some nostalgia and the going-out-of-business deals. They included everything from "Trump Won" caps for $9.99 to Trump pool floats for $19.99.   Trump stores first emerged during the 2016 campaign. But with the president now in his second and final term, store owners say there isn't as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened.   At least four stores have closed this year. The MAGA Mall, a big online retailer and wholesaler, reports sales of MAGA gear are down 30% compared to a presidential election year when Trump is on the ballot.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Trump fans Wes Alker and Joseph Flanagan pose at a going-out-of-business sale at a Trump store in suburban Philadelphia. Flanagan lives nearby and said he visited the store more than 25 times.
                
                    Frank Langfitt/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frank Langfitt/NPR
    

   
   "He's no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked," said Alker, who wore a gray T-shirt with a photo of former President Joe Biden and former Vice-President Kamala Harris which read, "Dumb and Dumber."   
   Trump's lame duck status isn't the only drag on demand. When the Bensalem store closed – it still maintains an online presence – Trump's average approval rating had already fallen from 50 % when he took office to 44 %.   Nine months later, when Bill Hays shut down his Trump super store outside of Knoxville, Tennessee, the president's approval rating had fallen five more points.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                This Trump store in a suburban Philadelphia strip mall is one of at least four that have closed this year as the president's merchandising appeal has dimmed.
                
                    Frank Langfitt/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frank Langfitt/NPR
    

   
   Hays said unpopular policies – such as DOGE's massive government staff cuts – have had an impact. He noticed that instead of immediately putting on their new Trump gear, more buyers asked for bags.   "People were not wearing their colors, so to speak, like they did before the (2024) election," said Hays, 80.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Trump merchandise has been big business. The MAGA Mall, a retailer and wholesaler, sells over a 1,000 MAGA, patriotic and religious products, including 400 different kinds of hats.
                
                    Frank Langfitt/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frank Langfitt/NPR
    

   
   When Hays opened his store in April 2024, business boomed. One day, he said, there was a line of 80 people out the door and sales hit $200,000 a month. By the time it closed in September, sales had fallen to just $20,000 a month.   "After the inauguration, I think a lot of people felt that their job was done," said Hays. "They didn't have to promote MAGA or Trump."   Hays still has a Trump store in the Tennessee tourist town of Gatlinburg. He's waiting to see how Christmas sales go before deciding its future.   Trump stores are a phenomenon. Other charismatic presidents such as Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama developed ardent followings, but didn't inspire brick-and-mortar merch outlets in red and blue states. Hays says Trump created such demand because he's a salesman - and he tells people what they want to hear.   
   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., sold a wide variety of products before it closed early this year. Items included an "Alligator Alcatraz" T-shirt, "Trump Won" caps and this patriotic Trump bear. The store continues to sell online.
                
                    Frank Langfitt/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frank Langfitt/NPR
    

   
   Ron Solomon, president of the MAGA Mall, says there are about 20 stores that specialize in Trump merchandise still in operation.   In Myrtle Beach, Rick Kligman sells items out of two stores, but he's trying to get rid of older material, stuffing $40 worth of merchandise into a grab bag that he sells for $9.99. He's concerned about the mid-terms and thinks a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate could turn off the more casual Trump consumer.   "I don't want to be sitting holding thousands and thousands of dollars of Trump merchandise and absolutely no possibility of selling it," said Kligman, 69.   Given term limits and Trump's age, retailers are diversifying beyond the Trump brand and embracing more patriotic products, including hats that say "We the People."    Solomon says this is a natural progression.   Eventually, Trump will leave the national stage. Unless a family member picks up the mantle, Solomon says the Trump merchandise business "will fade away."   Research by NPR's Susie Cummings.

schema.headline: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'

title: Backlash from attack ad upends Ohio gubernatorial race

      An ad from Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for governor shows his opponent's mother calling her a liar, amid accounts by Democrat Amy Acton of an abusive childhood.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    LEILA FADEL, HOST:  An attack ad from Ohio's Republican candidate for governor is itself being attacked by Democrats and some Republicans. They say it goes too far. The ad from Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign features the estranged mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton, someone who Acton says stood by while her stepfather abused her. George Shillcock of WOSU Public Media in Columbus is covering this. And just a warning here - we're about to discuss the sexual assault of a child. Good morning, George.GEORGE SHILLCOCK, BYLINE: Good morning, Leila.FADEL: So what is in this ad against Acton?SHILLCOCK: So the ad opens with her mother, Donna Arthur, warning people not to vote for her daughter and saying she has a problem.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)DONNA ARTHUR: She is a liar. She lies about her past.SHILLCOCK: Specifically, Arthur refutes stories that Acton has told for years about her difficult childhood. We found out Tuesday that Ramaswamy's campaign produced the ad.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)VIVEK RAMASWAMY: I would love for this race and this election to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans. And unfortunately, Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues.SHILLCOCK: He says he wants to debate Acton. And his campaign is spending millions to put this ad on air before Election Day.FADEL: Now, WOSU had the first interview with Acton about this ad. What did she say?SHILLCOCK: Yeah. She was on our talk show, All Sides with Amy Juravich. We already had her booked. And she explained first how she and her mother had been estranged for over 50 years. Court records produced by the campaign - and we verified all of this - show that they were homeless for a time and that Arthur lost custody of Acton and her little brother.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)AMY ACTON: I was removed from her at the age of 12 - my brother was 9 - for child abuse and neglect that got bad enough, we were actually living in a tent in the middle of winter.SHILLCOCK: Acton has said this before. But she also said that before she turned 12, her stepfather raped her. Acton's stepfather was charged with child rape, but left the state with Arthur before he could be tried. He's since died. And Acton says it was awful to see her mother used this way.FADEL: Let's talk a little more about what's at stake in this race. Ohio hasn't elected a Democratic governor in 20 years, but does that look like a possibility this time?SHILLCOCK: Well, Trump has won the state three times, but the Cook Political Report rates this as a toss-up. Bowling Green State University political science professor Robert Alexander thinks the ad could backfire on Ramaswamy by motivating Acton's supporters.ROBERT ALEXANDER: We know right now that it's a pretty tough environment for Republicans, and negative advertising can really stimulate that turnout among your core supporters. But again, it can also cause that backlash.SHILLCOCK: And he says this kind of advertising will likely lead to more of that.FADEL: So as a result of all this, the race now has the country's attention in a way it didn't last week. What has the reaction been?SHILLCOCK: Right. A rally in Ohio - Vice President JD Vance doubled down on the ad's liar language. He said he's, quote, "a little bit disgusted," end quote, when he sees Republicans who are whining about that ad. One of the Republicans criticizing the ad is former U.S. Ambassador Nikki Haley, who posted on X that Ramaswamy is a, quote, "bad guy." Libertarian candidate for Ohio Governor Don Kissick has called on Ramaswamy to drop out. And meanwhile, Trump and former President Barack Obama plan to come here to campaign for their party's candidates in the coming week.FADEL: That's George Shillcock of WOSU in Columbus, Ohio. Thank you, George.SHILLCOCK: Thank you.

title: Political communications expert discusses Vivek Ramaswamy's controversial ad
description: NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with political communications expert Jacob Neiheisel from the University of Buffalo about Vivek Ramaswamy's controve
body:
NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with political communications expert Jacob Neiheisel from the University of Buffalo about Vivek Ramaswamy's controversial ad.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  For more on Vivek Ramaswamy's ad, we've called Jacob Neiheisel. He's an associate professor of political science at the University of Buffalo where he specializes in political communications and campaigns. Professor, did this ad cross a line?JACOB NEIHEISEL: I think that's going to be up for the voters to decide, but it's certainly a very good example of a boomerang or a backlash effect, at least so far. We're seeing quite a bit of a reaction to it.MARTÍNEZ: Now, Ramasamy's campaign produced the ad, as we just heard, but say it had been a political action committee that wants him to be governor, would that have shielded him from the heat that it's getting?NEIHEISEL: It's quite possible. There is some research out there suggesting that, you know, PAC advertising that's overly negative but in support of a campaign can let a campaign get away with this kind of ad. And of course, one of the salient examples we have of a truly nasty ad being injected into a race is the Willie Horton ad. And even though that was something that was closely tied to the campaign, it wasn't actually run by the campaign itself.MARTÍNEZ: Yeah. And I also think of Michael Dukakis' ad when he was on a tank, and his helmet was ill fitting. That - now, that was a kind of a funny ad that wound up hurting him, but this one is definitely a lot more serious. I mean, what do you think? What are some lessons that need to be learned from an ad like this?NEIHEISEL: I think it really does suggest that if you're going to do this, it's best if somebody else be making the blows themselves. I think that that's a good lesson here. And I also think that, you know, it's really difficult to tell what the effect of this is going to be because you don't run this type of ad if you're doing well. You don't go this direction if things are looking good for your campaign. It truly is something of a Hail Mary. And so I think it's really just kind of solidifying a trend that we've seen in the polls already.MARTÍNEZ: Yeah. And what about the timing of this? I mean, if you're going to run an ad like this, I mean, does it - should it be a lot earlier so that if it backfires, you have time to try and recover and maybe figure out something else?NEIHEISEL: Yeah. That's a great question. I mean, we think that the timing of advertising when it hits is really quite important. Really, voters only are paying attention sort of the last two weeks of the campaign. I know it sounds strange to folks like us, but that's kind of their bandwidth for these types of things. And so if it's going to get in there and it's going to be something that affects the campaign, it's really going to be about now. So I'm not sure if running it earlier would've helped, but it certainly would've given it some distance if it did go wrong.MARTÍNEZ: Mentioned how you're a, you know, associate political science professor that specializes in political communications and campaigns. So, Professor, what makes a good campaign ad?NEIHEISEL: That's a fantastic question. And the answer that we have is, there's nothing that forever and always is something you should put in a political ad. Campaigns are a conversation, and it needs to be part of that conversation. And so we have a lot of research suggesting that it really depends. You know, there's no one magic thing that has to go in an ad. It depends on what the campaign is like and what the voters are demanding.MARTÍNEZ: So if a candidate wins the campaign, is it fair to say that all the ads were good ones because it got the candidate where the candidate wanted to go?NEIHEISEL: Oh, we're really tempted to say that. You know, ideally, we'd have access to things like the focus groups and the internal polls that the campaigns are doing to say that with some authority. But, yeah, we - it's hard to say, kind of, given how many they air and the overall tonnage that gets out there.MARTÍNEZ: Jacob Neiheisel is an associate political science professor at the University of Buffalo. Professor, thank you very much for your thoughts on this.NEIHEISEL: My pleasure. Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF DO MAKE SAY THINK'S "THE LANDLORD IS DEAD")MARTÍNEZ: NPR is tracking all the issues that matter to you, and you can find all of our coverage in one place on the NPR app. Download it today by going to npr.org/2026election.(SOUNDBITE OF DO MAKE SAY THINK'S "THE LANDLORD IS DEAD")

title: Kara Swisher on Elon Musk: 'He's unelected, unaccountable, enormously wealthy'
description:
A look at Elon Musk's wide-reaching influence
    
            
                
                Transcript
body:
A look at Elon Musk's wide-reaching influence
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6010616/nx-s1-9973913" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Podcaster Kara Swisher in Washington on June 11, 2026.
                
                    Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP
    

   
   Elon Musk says Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a possible merger, a move that could bring two of his biggest companies under one roof. But what is the business case for combining an electric vehicle manufacturer with a space and artificial intelligence company?   Longtime tech journalist Kara Swisher, who hosts the podcasts On and Pivot, spoke with Morning Edition host Steve Inskeep about Musk's expanding business empire and political influence.   "He's got to do something with Tesla as it descends downward," Swisher said, pointing to growing competition from Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers.   She argued that Musk missed an opportunity to develop an affordable electric car while competitors such as China's BYD expanded globally.   
   Swisher said data, AI and connectivity are increasingly central to Musk's businesses, though she questioned whether demand for computing power would hold up if the AI boom falters.   
   Swisher also discussed what Musk could face if Democrats regain control of Congress, as the billionaire spends hundreds of millions of dollars supporting Republican candidates.   "They could look into what happened at DOGE. I'd start there," Swisher said, referring to the Department of Government Efficiency. She also pointed to previous investigations involving Tesla crashes.   The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Musk ordered a slowdown of military-grade Starlink service used by Ukrainian forces, disrupting drone operations and air defenses. The decision reportedly caught Ukrainian officials and some in the Trump administration by surprise.   According to the same report by the WSJ, Musk said restrictions on the satellite network are determined by the U.S. military and ultimately the president. But Trump said he did not know who was responsible, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration had neither requested the slowdown nor known about it in advance.   
   "One single person who happens to be the world's richest man should not be making wartime decisions or decisions about our defense or anything else like that," Swisher said.   "He's unelected, unaccountable, enormously wealthy," she added. "One single person who has no guardrails on him to be able to make these decisions that results in the deaths of people across the globe."   NPR has repeatedly sought comment from Musk, who has a standing invitation to speak with the network. NPR also reached out to SpaceX for comment on this story.   
   The digital version of this interview was edited by Treye Green.

title: High health costs squeeze workers, even if you have good insurance through a job
description: The latest survey from health research o
body:
The latest survey from health research organization KFF on employer-sponsored health insurance finds that premiums went up about 5%.
                
                    The Good Brigade/Digital Vision/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        The Good Brigade/Digital Vision/Getty Images
    

   
   Joseph Babbitt of Springfield, Mo. has a pretty good deal when it comes to health insurance. He works as a senior financial controller for West Plains Veterinary Supply, which employs about 50 people and distributes pet food, toys and vet supplies across the region.   
   Like about 157 million Americans, Babbitt gets insurance through his job. Unlike most Americans, his job has exceptionally generous benefits. "Our owners are very nice — they give all of our employees health care and they pay for it," he says. The company offers several different plan options and covers most or all of the monthly premium cost.      So why, even with free premiums, does it still feel like health costs are way too expensive? "Everybody talks about health care and how much it's costing them," says Babbitt. He explains that even without monthly premiums, a high deductible can be brutal — that's the amount the patient has to spend out-of-pocket before the insurance company starts paying for doctors visits and procedures, etc.   
   Now age 60, he remembers a time when it wasn't so bad. "Back in the '90s, our deductibles were $250 [or] $500 — now they're $5,000," he says. "That seems like a lot."   "We are the only country on our planet that forces people into bankruptcy because they get sick," he adds.   The cost of a new car, every year   Health care costs are rising fast in the U.S., and even workers with solid health care benefits through work are feeling it, according to an annual survey of nearly 2,000 employers about their health benefits. The report was published Thursday by KFF, a nonpartisan health research organization.   "The average health insurance premium for a family of four is now $28,000, which is just a ton of money," says Matthew Rae, associate director for the Health Care Marketplace Program at KFF. "It's basically the cost of a new car every year just to keep a family of four insured." Of that total for family premiums, workers pay about $7,000 per year on average and employers pay the rest.   A glimmer of positivity is that the costs for plans isn't growing as fast as it has in years past, he explains. "We're seeing a 5% increase in family health insurance premiums, which continues a period of modest growth," he says. That increase is roughly on par with worker wages and inflation.   
   However, "a 5% increase on a big number is still a lot of money," Rae points out. Plus, the growth for the portion of the premium costs that workers pay was 9%. "If this is the beginning of a shift of costs onto workers, that would be a big deal in terms of affordability," he says.   "We are asking people to chip in a lot of money," Rae adds. "Many people are committing a big chunk of their income to health insurance."   The uninsured rate is rising    Another report published Thursday demonstrates the way these high costs affect people's health. The survey, conducted every two years by the Commonwealth Fund, a nonprofit foundation that supports independent research, is entitled "The State of Health Insurance Coverage in 2026."   Even for workers fortunate enough to have health benefits, "about 43% of them said that they didn't get health care because of cost over the past year, and about 31% reported that they had medical debt," says Sara Collins, lead author of the report.   Another key finding was that the overall uninsured rate rose in the last two years. Collins says that's significant but not surprising, because of federal policy decisions like letting extra federal subsidies for people enrolled in Affordable Care Act plans expire, and people losing Medicaid after the pandemic emergency ended.   
   Federal data shows millions of people have lost health coverage already from either Medicaid or the ACA marketplaces. When work requirements take effect next year, millions more people are projected to lose Medicaid.   "There is a, I think, a strong feeling across the country that something probably does need to be done to the situation that people are facing in their health and health insurance — both on the cost side and then also on these coverage losses," Collins says.   "We asked people whether the federal government has a responsibility to ensure that all Americans have coverage and nearly three quarters said yes to that — that included about 45% of Republicans, 93% of Democrats and 76% of independents."
